statedGuarantee: The PEA (Policy-Execution-Authorization) architecture claims Goal Integrity: every executed action (i) carries a cryptographically signed, TTL-bound, single-use capability token issued only by a deterministic Authorization kernel (T1 Non-Bypassability, T3 Safety under Adversarial Input, T4 Type Preservation), (ii) has a capability drawn from MinimalCapSet(IntentType, PolicyContext) for the authorizing intent (T5 Intent-Safe Execution), (iii) is traceable to the originating natural-language request by a SHA-256 lineage anchor plus an independently computed embedding-similarity score at or above a drift threshold, and matches no Shutdown-Resistance Blacklist rule (T6 Goal-Integrity), and (iv) produces output that passes an Output Semantic Gate combining deterministic HOPS pattern rules with a KxIxP coercion calculus and an independently deployed evaluator LLM. Delegated tokens may not exceed parent scope (T2). All six theorems are explicitly conditional on assumptions A1-A12.
advertisedRhetoric: "PEA decouples intent generation, authorization, and execution into independent layers connected via cryptographically constrained capability tokens." / "structural enforcement converts the AI safety problem from a probabilistic behavioral question into a conditionally sound system property" / "the same conceptual shift that mandatory access control represented in operating systems: from 'agents should behave safely' to 'the system enforces safety regardless of agent behavior.'" The paper further aligns itself with a verified kernel: "PEA adopts the same verification strategy and handles LLM non-determinism via oracle abstraction."
tierSpan: Create an alternative execution path bypassing the Authorization layer (Assumption A3: no bypass path exists).
cheapestDefeat: Worked explicitly. (1) The guarantee: no side-effecting action occurs without a valid signed capability token whose capability lies in MinimalCapSet, and no output is delivered without passing the OSG. (2) The mechanism that must fail: not the HMAC-SHA256 signature, but the Execution layer's in-process dispatch gate - "Execution Layer: validates tokens and dispatches approved actions. Policy-agnostic and decision-minimal: it executes what a valid token authorizes, nothing more." Non-bypassability of that gate is asserted, not built: it is Assumption A3, and the T1 proof rests entirely on it ("The only rule producing side-effecting state transitions is INTENT-STEP, which requires ... as a premise"). (3) The cheapest adversary action: reach the effector by any path that never calls the dispatcher - a tool implementation that performs its own file or socket I/O, a child process, an interpreter or shell invoked under a legitimately granted 'execute' capability, or any library the executing tool loads. No signature forgery, no cryptanalysis and no kernel exploit is required; the crypto binds only what a compliant dispatcher accepts. (4) The mechanism that action defeats is an application-level chokepoint. No netns, seccomp, LSM, container, firewall or hypervisor boundary appears anywhere in the paper; the prototype dispatcher runs against a "mock environment" and integration is offered as "A sidecar deployment pattern allows PEA enforcement to be applied to existing AI systems' tool calls without full rewrite." Weakest link = T3. This is precisely the protocol's worked example: signed capability mandates enforced by an in-process hook score T3, not T1.
placementSpan: Crucially, the adversary model treats the Policy LLM as an untrusted component by default. Security properties are proved for all possible Policy LLM outputs, including worst-case adversarial outputs-not merely for expected or well-behaved outputs.

coverageSpans.E1: L 1 ∈ { file, database, api, payment, credential } ... L 2 ∈ { read, write, execute, delete, export } ... This taxonomy yields at most 100 distinct capability combinations. -- taken with the tested invariant "Token Enforcement Rate | 100% | All executed actions presented a valid signed token". File write/delete/export is a first-class named capability class and T1 is a universal over all executed actions; nothing in the text carves file writes out, so on the charitable reading E1 is covered at T3.
coverageSpans.E2: Execution Layer (token validator, action dispatcher in mock environment, Revocation Bitmap) -- the words subprocess, child process, process tree and descendant appear nowhere in the paper. 'execute' exists as an L2 capability verb, so a declared execute action is gated, but nothing mediates what a spawned process then does. DEPTH RULE caps this at partial.
coverageSpans.E3: PEA does not claim to eliminate covert channels-it claims to reduce the covert channel attack surface to the authorized information set. -- and, in the explicit list of what PEA does not guarantee: "That covert channels within the authorized capability scope are eliminated- A 10 A_{10} explicitly bounds this residual." Top-level egress is gated by the 'api' capability class and screened by the OSG, but the stated contract excludes the covert channel through which exfiltration is achieved, and descendant egress is never addressed. COVERT-CHANNEL RULE: partial, never covered.
coverageSpans.E4: Never named in the paper. A version-control push would have to be dispatched as an 'api' or 'execute' triple from the closed capability vocabulary and would then require a token, so the guarantee reaches declared instances; but a push performed by a git subprocess under a granted execute capability is a descendant path the paper does not mediate. Partial.
coverageSpans.E5: Never named in the paper. A package install dispatched as an execute/api action would require a token, but third-party install hooks and the network activity they perform are never discussed and are by construction descendants of the dispatched process. Per the depth rule (E5 covered only if install hooks and their network activity are mediated), partial.
coverageSpans.E6: L 1 ∈ { file, database, api, payment, credential } -- credential is an explicit first-class capability class and "Integrating the IdentityStore for clearance lookup." is a named integration step. But there is no published credential list: "The MinimalCapSet table is a static, human-maintained configuration mapping each IntentType to the minimal set of" capability triples, and the paper concedes "That MinimalCapSet specifications are complete- A 9 A_{9} is a deployment obligation, not a theorem." Undefined list, so capped at partial.
coverageSpans.E7: Assumptions: A4 (all delegation through Authorization), A5 (Auth enforces attenuation). -- delegation is genuinely addressed by T2 and tested ("multi-agent delegation escalation attempts" is one of the five attack classes in the 10,000-trial corpus). But the paper files the general case under future work: "multi-model orchestration with cross-model delegation graph bounds". A sub-agent brought up outside the token-request path is unmediated. Partial.

schneider.surrogate: A per-action reference-monitor safety property a monitor can enforce: no state-changing transition occurs unless the actor presents an unexpired, unredeemed, correctly signed capability token whose (L1,L2,L3) triple is a member of the static MinimalCapSet table for the declared IntentType, whose lineage anchor equals the session NLR hash, that matches no Shutdown-Resistance Blacklist rule and no HOPS output pattern. Every conjunct is a decidable predicate over the current step plus finite accumulated state. This is what T1-T5 actually prove.
schneider.objective: 'Goal Integrity' as advertised - that executed actions are semantically faithful to the user's originating intent and that outputs carry no implicit coercion or unauthorized disclosure. Not enforceable in Schneider's sense: the drift check is an embedding-similarity proxy above a tunable threshold, the OSG Track 2 check is an LLM judgment the authors themselves downgrade to a probabilistic invariant ("Safety Invariant I 13 I_{13} is therefore stated as a ( 1 − ϵ ) (1-\epsilon) -probability invariant rather than a deterministic one"), and the residual exfiltration objective is an information-flow hyperproperty the paper explicitly declines to close. The paper is unusually candid about the split - "Traceability ≠ Correctness" and "That all harmful actions are prevented-only that prohibited and intent-divergent capabilities are enforced structurally" - but candour about the gap does not close it.

notes:
FULL TEXT OBTAINED. arXiv:2604.23646v1 [cs.AI] 26 Apr 2026, 'Structural Enforcement of Goal Integrity in AI Agents via Separation-of-Powers Architecture / The PEA Model: Policy-Execution-Authorization for Agentic Misalignment Resistance', single author Rong Xiang (aiegisafety@outlook.com). The LaTeXML HTML (v1, the only version) was fetched in full and read end to end: all 8 sections, theorems T1-T6 with proof sketches and load-bearing-assumption table, evaluation E1-E3, assumption stress testing, ablation, policy-variation experiment, limitations and related work. Coding is from the full text, not the abstract.

WHY THIS PAPER MATTERS TO T-12: it is the cleanest corpus instance of the crypto-rhetoric / in-process-execution mismatch. The token machinery is real (HMAC-SHA256, TTL 30-300s, single-use, versioned against system state to defeat replay) and the 8-step authorization pipeline is a genuine deterministic kernel sitting OUTSIDE the LLM - a stronger design than most. But the plane that redeems the token is an in-process dispatcher whose non-bypassability is imported as Assumption A3 rather than constructed. The paper is explicit that A3 is load-bearing for T1, T3 and T5, which is exactly why even the charitable coder must stop at T3: the honesty locates the gap, it does not close it. The seL4 analogy in Sections 6.6 and 7.1 is aspirational - seL4's dispatch boundary is enforced by hardware page tables under a machine-checked kernel; PEA's is enforced by the assumption that no other code path exists.

TIER - WHERE I WAS UNCERTAIN: a T2 reading is simply unavailable on this text (no OS, kernel, sandbox or namespace mechanism is described; the Execution layer is a 'token validator, action dispatcher in mock environment'). A T1 reading would require that defeating the guarantee require defeating the signature, which it does not. T3 is the only defensible score, and I do not think a more charitable reading exists.

COVERAGE - WHERE I WAS UNCERTAIN, FOR THE ADJUDICATOR: (a) E1 is the single 'covered' cell and the closest call in this coding. Charitable case: file x {write, delete, export} is a named first-class capability class, T1 is a universal over all executed actions, and the tested invariant is 100% token enforcement across 10,000 trials. Uncharitable case: a coder applying the descendant test uniformly would score E1 'partial' too, because the paper is silent on what a dispatched tool does after dispatch. I resolved in the authors' favour per the charitable stance since nothing contradicts file-write mediation - but this is the cell most likely to flip on adjudication.
(b) E4 and E5 are effectors the paper never names. I scored them 'partial' rather than 'not-covered' because the closed capability vocabulary would subsume a declared push or install as an api/execute triple, so the guarantee reaches SOME instances. An adjudicator applying 'a system that simply does not address an effector scores not-covered' strictly would score both not-covered; that reading is defensible and I flag it explicitly.
(c) E6 is capped at partial purely by the published-credential-list rule. 'credential' IS an L1 capability class - better than most systems in this corpus - but MinimalCapSet is a deployment-supplied, human-maintained table and A9 is conceded to be 'a deployment obligation, not a theorem', so there is no published list to score against.

EVIDENCE GRADE L2, NOT HIGHER: a prototype was built and run (Policy layer GPT-class LLM at temperature 0.7, Z3 for the SMT gate, embedding drift detector at theta_drift = 0.82, an independently deployed evaluator LLM for OSG Track 2) against three constructed datasets (Attack Corpus 10,000 / Drift Dataset 5,000 / Coercion Dataset 3,000). There is no code URL, no repository, no artifact appendix, no named model and no dataset release, and the action dispatcher runs in a 'mock environment' - so enforcement is confirmed behaviourally on a simulated action surface, not on real files, sockets or processes. No reproducible bypass is demonstrated, so not L3.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY WORTH FLAGGING: the abstract states 'implicit coercion detection at 84.7percent recall' while Table E3 reports overall Recall 88.2% and Implicit Threat Detection Rate 84.7% - the abstract conflates the two. The abstract also reports the Hard Auth ablation as '(34.8percent attack success rate)' where Section 5.6's table gives 34.8% ASR / +30.9pp; both are internally consistent but the abstract's phrasing invites misquotation as a 34.8pp effect. Section 5.6's table is authoritative. Section 2.4 also contains a dangling sentence: 'We seek to guarantee Goal Integrity: .' - the definition after the colon is missing in the HTML render.

A STRUCTURAL CONTRADICTION THE ADJUDICATOR SHOULD SEE: Section 3.1 treats the Policy layer output as untrusted and Section 2.2 grants the adversary arbitrary Policy LLM outputs - yet the OSG Track 2 backstop, the Soft Auth evaluator and the drift-similarity model are themselves models, mitigated only by a deployment requirement of model diversity ('Deploying three model-diversity-compliant LLM components (Policy, Soft Auth, OSG Track 2)'). The untrusted boundary is drawn around one LLM while three others sit inside the trusted computing base, and correlated failure across them is never discussed. Note also theta_drift is given as 'default: 0.40' in Section 3.4 but as 0.82 in the Section 5.2 experimental setup and in T6's evaluation; the two are never reconciled.

PLACEMENT: primary A3 is unambiguous - the motivating threat is agentic misalignment in which 'the Policy layer itself is the origin of the harmful intent', and E2 directly tests it (5,000 tasks where 'the Policy LLM is incentivized to produce high-similarity but semantically divergent intents'). A2 is addressed and partially tested (NLRs, retrieved context, tool outputs and conversation history are all declared adversarial; direct prompt injection is an E1 attack class) and A1 likewise (token replay). A4 and A5 are explicitly out of scope: the Authorization rule engine, the cryptographic primitives, the Hard Auth rule set, the MinimalCapSet table and the Control Token Store are all assumed untamperable at runtime, and the Audit Log is assumed unmodifiable.
